## Guided Tutorial 5.1: Adding Text, Date, and Logical Columns

**Context and objective.** In this tutorial, you will prepare two of the Tables in your analysis workbook for the lookups and summaries that follow. On the Item Table, you will extract each item's product type from its code and test that every code has the expected form. On the SalesInvoice Table, you will assign each invoice to a fiscal year, a fiscal quarter, and a period label, measure its payment terms in days, and use logical functions to group the terms and test them. Each new column is a calculated column, so it fills every row and extends to rows added by a refresh.

**Prerequisites.** You need the Charles River Furniture Analysis workbook from Chapter 4, with the SalesInvoice, SalesInvoiceLine, Item, and PromotionProgram Tables loaded by Power Query.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Extract the product type from the item code.** The product type is the middle part of the code, three characters starting at the fifth.

a. Go to the **Item** worksheet. Click the first empty cell to the right of the last header, LifecycleStatus, type `ProductType`, and press Enter.
b. In the first data row of the new column, enter `=MID([@ItemCode],5,3)`.
c. Check a few rows: FUR-DSK-0075 should return DSK, and FUR-SDB-0002 should return SDB.

Every item now carries a three-letter product type. @tbl-05-03 lists the Furniture product types and their codes; other groups have their own codes, such as PND for pendant lights and RUG for rugs.

| Code | Furniture product type | Code | Furniture product type |
|---|---|---|---|
| BKC | Bookcase | DSK | Desk |
| BNH | Bench | NGT | Nightstand |
| CON | Console table | SDB | Sideboard |
| CTB | Coffee table | TBL | Dining table |

: Furniture product type codes {#tbl-05-03}

**Step 2. Test that every item code has the expected form.** A code of the form GRP-TYP-9999 has twelve characters, with hyphens in the fourth and eighth positions.

a. Add another column, `CodeCheck`, with this formula:

   ```
   =AND(LEN([@ItemCode])=12,MID([@ItemCode],4,1)="-",MID([@ItemCode],8,1)="-")
   ```

b. On the **Analysis** worksheet, type `Item codes failing the check` in A40 and enter `=COUNTIF(Item[CodeCheck],FALSE)` in B40.

Every item Charles River sells passes the check, so B40 shows zero, which means the product type formula can be trusted for every item.

@fig-05-02 shows the Item Table with both new columns.

![The Item Table with the Product Type Extracted from the Item Code.](/visuals/svg/fig-05-02-item-product-type.svg){#fig-05-02 fig-alt="A mock of the Item Table in the analysis workbook, showing ItemID, ItemCode, ItemName, and ItemGroup for several Furniture items, and two new calculated columns: ProductType, which holds the middle three letters of each item code, such as DSK for a desk and SDB for a sideboard, and CodeCheck, which is TRUE for every row. The formula bar shows =MID([@ItemCode],5,3). The two new columns are outlined."}

**Step 3. Assign each invoice to a fiscal period.** Charles River's fiscal year is the calendar year.

a. Go to the **SalesInvoice** worksheet. In the first empty column after PaymentDate, add a column `FiscalYear` with the formula `=YEAR([@InvoiceDate])`.
b. Add a column `FiscalQuarter` with the formula `=ROUNDUP(MONTH([@InvoiceDate])/3,0)`.
c. Add a column `Period` with the formula `=[@FiscalYear]&"-Q"&[@FiscalQuarter]`, which returns labels such as 2026-Q4.

Each invoice now carries its fiscal year, its quarter, and a single label that combines them. The label sorts correctly because the year comes first.

**Step 4. Measure the payment terms in days.** Subtracting the invoice date from the due date gives the number of days a customer has to pay.

a. Add a column `DaysToDue` with the formula `=[@DueDate]-[@InvoiceDate]`.
b. If Excel formats the result as a date, change the column's number format to **General** or **Number** with no decimals.

Each invoice now shows its payment terms as a whole number of days. @fig-05-03 shows the SalesInvoice Table with the four new columns.

![The SalesInvoice Table with Fiscal Period and Payment Terms Columns.](/visuals/svg/fig-05-03-salesinvoice-periods.svg){#fig-05-03 fig-alt="A mock of the SalesInvoice Table in the analysis workbook, showing SalesInvoiceID, InvoiceNumber, InvoiceDate, and DueDate for several invoices, and four new calculated columns: FiscalYear, FiscalQuarter, Period, which joins the two into a label such as 2024-Q1, and DaysToDue, the number of days between the invoice date and the due date. The formula bar shows the formula for Period. The new columns are outlined."}

**Step 5. Group and test the payment terms.** Logical functions turn the terms into a label for reporting and a check for review.

a. Add a column `TermsGroup` with this formula, which places each invoice in one of three bands:

   ```
   =IFS([@DaysToDue]<=30,"Up to 30 days",[@DaysToDue]<=60,"31 to 60 days",TRUE,"Over 60 days")
   ```

b. Add a column `StandardTerms` with this formula, which is TRUE when the terms are one of the four that Charles River offers:

   ```
   =OR([@DaysToDue]=30,[@DaysToDue]=45,[@DaysToDue]=60,[@DaysToDue]=90)
   ```

c. On the **Analysis** worksheet, type `Invoices with nonstandard terms` in A39.
d. In B39, enter `=COUNTIF(SalesInvoice[StandardTerms],FALSE)`.

B39 shows zero: every invoice has one of the four standard terms, so no due date appears to have been typed by hand. Most invoices fall in the two lower bands of TermsGroup, and only a few hundred have terms longer than 60 days.

**Step 6. Check the period labels.** Open the filter list on the Period column and read the values it shows.

The Period column holds one label for each quarter of the three fiscal years in the data, from 2024-Q1 to 2026-Q4. A label outside that range would point to an invoice dated outside the period of the extract.

**Step 7. Record the new columns.**

a. On the **Documentation** worksheet, add the new calculated columns to the Calculated columns entry, each with its formula: ProductType and CodeCheck on Item, and FiscalYear, FiscalQuarter, Period, DaysToDue, TermsGroup, and StandardTerms on SalesInvoice.
b. Add the check in B39 to the entry that describes the Analysis worksheet.
c. Save the workbook.

The Documentation worksheet now accounts for every column this tutorial added, so a reviewer can see how each value was calculated.

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- every item has a three-letter ProductType, and no item code fails the CodeCheck test;
- every invoice has a Period label from 2024-Q1 to 2026-Q4;
- every invoice has a TermsGroup label, and no invoice fails the StandardTerms test;
- the Documentation worksheet lists the new columns.

The product type and the period are the two attributes the controller's question needs that the invoice lines do not carry. The next tutorial brings them onto the lines.
